title: Budućnost i naredbe
theme: Tomorrow uses ću, commands split blunt and polite, and moći, morati, trebati, and htjeti cover can, must, need, and want.
reviewerNotes: Mold polish re-applied after concurrent Bosnian-editor overwrite. Full-sentence theme; no verb-machine voice; ću second-place only (no Ću-first); blunt/polite Radi/Radite and Pij/Pijte; café modals; aspect bleed trimmed from pattern; table One form / Sister form; Chapter 12 clitic tease kept light. Bosnian retained/checked: ću/ćeš/će/ćemo/ćete/će, Radi/Radite, Pij/Pijte, Idi/Idite, mogu/moram/trebam/hoću and polite sisters. Still draft pending human publish decision. whyHere.heading: Why you are here
whyHere.body: Today you learn three café tools that travel together. Future uses short ću, ćeš, će, ćemo, ćete, će plus an infinitive, as in Ti ćeš piti kahvu for you will drink coffee. Commands have a blunt form and a polite form, as in Radi versus Radite. Want, must, need, and can sit on htjeti, morati, trebati, and moći. English spreads these across will, please, and helper verbs. Bosnian keeps them short. This chapter is that bundle, and clitic second place waits for Chapter 12.

englishLies.heading: Why English lies
englishLies.body: English lies because will, please, can, must, and need feel like separate drawers. You will drink, drink please, you must drink, and you can drink each grab different helpers and tones. Bosnian reuses a tiny future helper, a command ending, and four everyday modal verbs. Hoću overlaps with wanting. Moram is I must. Trebam is I need. Mogu is I can. Schools may split budućnost, imperativ, and modalni glagoli onto three posters. In this notebook they share one day because you meet them in the same café turn.

knownLine.heading: A line you already say
knownLine.body: Book 1 already gave you Ana’s line Želim kahvu, which means I want coffee. Wanting also rides on htjeti, so Hoću kahvu is a blunt cousin you will hear. Emir can answer Ja ću piti kahvu when he means I will drink coffee. Amira can soften a command to Molim, radite or keep it blunt with Radi. Today you map those moves without inventing English word-for-word copies.
knownLine.speaker: Emir

pattern.heading: The pattern
pattern.body: Future is a short helper plus an infinitive. Ja ću piti, ti ćeš piti, on će piti, mi ćemo piti, vi ćete piti, oni će piti. The helper likes second place, so Ja ću piti kahvu and Piti ću kahvu both appear, and a naked Ću at the start of a sentence is wrong. Commands cut to a short stem for one friend, as in Radi, Pij, and Idi, and they add -te for polite or plural, as in Radite, Pijte, and Idite. The modal row is small. Mogu means I can. Moram means I must. Trebam means I need. Hoću means I want. Keep the Chapter 8 who-endings on those modals, and leave the finish of the action for another day.

howYouGuess.heading: The pests
howYouGuess.body: Three pests will trip you today. The first pest is stacking English will onto a present form, as in will pijem, or parking ću at the front of the sentence. Use Ja ću piti or Piti ću. The second pest is barking Radi at a stranger when Radite or a soft molim would fit. Blunt is fine with friends. Polite -te is safer with new people. The third pest is mixing trebati and morati. Moram is duty pressure. Trebam is need. Hoću is want, and it is not the same soft wish as želim in every room, even when both translate want.

trick.heading: The bit that tricks you
trick.body: The trap is to treat ću as optional flavor on a present sentence, or to put ću first. Ja ću piti is future. Pijem is present. Ću piti with nothing before ću breaks the second-place habit Chapter 12 will name. The other trap is to hear Hoću kahvu and decide Bosnian lost želim. Both live. Želim often sounds like a plain want from Book 1. Hoću can sound stronger or more blunt. For commands, do not add please into the verb ending. Molim is a separate softener beside Radite.

nerd.heading: Why it's like this
nerd.body:
Old English is the English of England about a thousand years ago, not a class you missed. It had its own future hacks and command forms, and later English rebuilt future with will and going to. You speak that rebuilt kit. Please stayed a separate soft word, the way molim still sits beside a command in Bosnian.

Bosnian future helpers are worn-down bits of htjeti, the want verb, which is why ću smells like wanting while it marks time. Commands keep an old short stem. The modal row is just high-frequency verbs that take infinitives the way English can and must do. Schools split the posters. Café talk bundles them, so this chapter does too.

items.explanation: Future is ću in second place plus infinitive.
Ćeš cannot open the sentence. Doći ćeš keeps it second.
Short blunt form for one friend.
Morati carries duty. Trebati is need.

items.prompt: Someone says will pijem kahvu. What is the fix?
items.explanation: Future wants ću in second place plus infinitive.

items.prompt: Softening a polite command often adds which word?
items.explanation: Molim sits beside Radite or Pijte. It is not baked into the ending.
Htjeti gives Hoću for want. Trebam is need. Moram is duty.

questions.question: Polite command. Drink the coffee.
questions.explanation: Add -te for polite or plural. Pij is blunt for one friend.

questions.question: How do you build I will drink coffee?
options: Ću piti kahvu with ću first
questions.explanation: Helper ću sits in second place plus infinitive piti.

questions.question: Radi versus Radite is which contrast?
questions.explanation: Commands add -te for polite or plural.

questions.question: Moram ići marks which meaning?
questions.explanation: Morati is duty. Trebati is need. Hoću is want.

questions.question: What comes next after future, commands, and modals?
options: Chapter 1 piles again as the only topic
questions.explanation: Chapter 12 is enklitike. Ja se zovem works. Se zovem does not.

next.body: You now have ću for tomorrow, blunt versus polite commands, and the café row mogu, moram, trebam, and hoću. Chapter 12 is why little words like se and sam hunt second place in the sentence. Ja se zovem works. Se zovem does not. That habit finishes the grammar walk before the English-shaped mistakes review.
